Task_2_Trust_Context_Validation.decision_path: Matches hardcoded package string to hardcoded category -> Checks if cert is TRUSTED -> Assumes LEGITIMATE_USE
Task_2_Trust_Context_Validation.conclusion: trust_context_engine.py relies purely on hardcoded assumptions and scaffolding, lacking any dynamic app store lookups or heuristic reputation scoring.

Task_3_False_Positive_Challenge.VLC.apk: A researcher would argue that malware often disguises itself as media players to obtain overlay permissions. Trusting it just because its package name matches org.videolan.vlc is trivial to spoof.
Task_3_False_Positive_Challenge.Termux.apk: Termux is an open-source terminal, but a malicious dropper could easily impersonate it. Blindly trusting it based on category invites supply-chain abuse.
Task_3_False_Positive_Challenge.Element.apk: While Element needs SMS for verification, ignoring its SMS parsing logic entirely because of 'TRUSTED' cert ignores the threat of legitimate apps being compromised or exhibiting dual-use spyware behavior.
Task_3_False_Positive_Challenge.NewPipe.apk: Same as VLC, open-source apps are frequently repackaged. Trusting it based on category assumptions without deep byte-code validation is a massive blind spot.
Task_3_False_Positive_Challenge.SecureBank_Official.apk: Banks sometimes bundle risky SDKs (e.g., location trackers). Assuming a bank app is 100% benign ignores privacy violations and potential supply chain attacks.
Task_3_False_Positive_Challenge.SecureBank_Plus.apk: No disagreement. It correctly identifies the phishing overlay.
Task_3_False_Positive_Challenge.SecureBank_Clone.apk: No disagreement. It correctly flags the clone.
